BEGINNER1. Typing Function Parameters and Returns

Definition

Every function parameter should have an explicit type, since TypeScript cannot infer it purely from how the function is defined. Return types are usually inferred, but can be annotated too.

function add(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a + b;
}

function greet(name: string): string {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}

add(2, 3);        // 5
// add("2", 3);   // ❌ Error: Argument of type 'string' is not
//                   assignable to parameter of type 'number'
Why annotate parameters: Without annotations, parameters implicitly become any (or cause an error under noImplicitAny), silently disabling type checking for that function.

Inferred vs Explicit Return Types

// Inferred - TypeScript figures out the return is number
function square(n: number) {
    return n * n;
}

// Explicit - documents intent, catches accidental mismatches
function cube(n: number): number {
    return n * n * n;
}

BEGINNER2. Optional, Default, and Rest Parameters

Optional Parameters

function buildName(first: string, last?: string): string {
    return last ? `${first} ${last}` : first;
}

buildName("Madonna");          // "Madonna"
buildName("John", "Smith");    // "John Smith"

Default Parameters

function createUser(name: string, role: string = "member"): string {
    return `${name} (${role})`;
}

createUser("Ana");             // "Ana (member)"
createUser("Ana", "admin");    // "Ana (admin)"

Rest Parameters

function sum(...numbers: number[]): number {
    return numbers.reduce((total, n) => total + n, 0);
}

sum(1, 2, 3);        // 6
sum(1, 2, 3, 4, 5);  // 15
⚠️ Common Pitfall: Optional and default parameters must be declared after all required parameters. Rest parameters must always come last.

BEGINNER3. Function Type Expressions

You can describe the "shape" of a function — its parameters and return type — as its own type, useful for callbacks and variables that hold functions.

type MathOperation = (a: number, b: number) => number;

const multiply: MathOperation = (a, b) => a * b;
const divide: MathOperation = (a, b) => a / b;

function calculate(a: number, b: number, operation: MathOperation): number {
    return operation(a, b);
}

calculate(10, 5, multiply);   // 50
calculate(10, 5, divide);     // 2

Naming Parameters in Function Types

Parameter names in a function type are just documentation — only the position and type matter for compatibility.

type Logger = (message: string, level: "info" | "error") => void;

const consoleLogger: Logger = (msg, lvl) => {
    console.log(`[${lvl.toUpperCase()}] ${msg}`);
};

INTERMEDIATE4. Arrow Functions vs Function Declarations

Function Declaration: 
function add(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a + b;
}
// Hoisted - can be called before defined
// Has its own 'this' binding
Arrow Function: 
const add = (a: number, b: number): number => {
    return a + b;
};
// Not hoisted
// Inherits 'this' from enclosing scope

Typing Arrow Functions Assigned to a Variable

const isEven: (n: number) => boolean = (n) => n % 2 === 0;

// More commonly, let the function type alias do the work:
type Predicate = (n: number) => boolean;
const isOdd: Predicate = (n) => n % 2 !== 0;

Function Expressions

const subtract = function (a: number, b: number): number {
    return a - b;
};

INTERMEDIATE5. Function Overloads

Overloads let a single function name accept different combinations of parameter types and return correspondingly different types, more precisely than a union type alone would allow.

// Overload signatures
function makeDate(timestamp: number): Date;
function makeDate(month: number, day: number, year: number): Date;
// Implementation signature (not directly callable from outside)
function makeDate(monthOrTimestamp: number, day?: number, year?: number): Date {
    if (day !== undefined && year !== undefined) {
        return new Date(year, monthOrTimestamp - 1, day);
    }
    return new Date(monthOrTimestamp);
}

makeDate(1_700_000_000_000);   // ✅ OK - matches first overload
makeDate(8, 15, 2024);         // ✅ OK - matches second overload
// makeDate(8, 15);            // ❌ Error: No overload expects 2 arguments
💡 Tip: The implementation signature is never visible to callers — only the overload signatures are. It must be general enough to handle every overload's parameter combination.
⚠️ Common Pitfall: If a union type parameter would express the same intent, prefer it over overloads — overloads add complexity and should be reserved for cases where the return type genuinely depends on which combination of arguments was passed.

INTERMEDIATE6. this Parameters

TypeScript lets you declare the expected type of this as a fake first parameter, purely for type-checking — it's erased at compile time and never appears in the compiled JavaScript.

interface Button {
    label: string;
    onClick(this: Button, event: string): void;
}

const button: Button = {
    label: "Submit",
    onClick(this: Button, event: string) {
        console.log(`${this.label} clicked: ${event}`);
    }
};

button.onClick("click");   // OK - called with correct 'this'

// const detached = button.onClick;
// detached("click");      // ❌ Error if strict this-checking flags this misuse
Real-world use case: DOM event handlers and jQuery-style APIs where this refers to the element that triggered the event benefit from explicit this typing to prevent accidental detachment bugs.

INTERMEDIATE7. Callback Parameter Typing

function fetchData(
    url: string,
    onSuccess: (data: string) => void,
    onError: (error: Error) => void
): void {
    // simulate an async call
    const success = true;
    if (success) {
        onSuccess("response data");
    } else {
        onError(new Error("Request failed"));
    }
}

fetchData(
    "/api/data",
    (data) => console.log("Got:", data),
    (err) => console.error("Failed:", err.message)
);

Array Method Callbacks

const numbers: number[] = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];

// TypeScript infers 'n' as number from the array's element type
const doubled = numbers.map((n) => n * 2);
const evens = numbers.filter((n) => n % 2 === 0);
const total = numbers.reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0);

ADVANCED8. Void Return vs Contextual Typing Quirks

A function typed to return void can still be assigned an implementation that returns something else — as long as that return value is ignored.

type VoidCallback = () => void;

// This is allowed even though the arrow function returns a boolean;
// TypeScript trusts you to discard the value.
const onClick: VoidCallback = () => {
    return true;   // ✅ allowed, but the 'true' is discarded by contract
};

const items: number[] = [];
// Array.prototype.push returns a number, but forEach expects void callbacks
[1, 2, 3].forEach((n) => items.push(n));   // ✅ OK, push's number return is ignored
⚠️ Common Pitfall: This "void-returning function accepts non-void implementations" rule exists so common patterns like arr.forEach(x => arr2.push(x)) compile — but it means void is not as strict a guarantee as it might first appear.

ADVANCED9. Higher-Order Functions with Generics

Functions that accept or return other functions often need generics to preserve type information across the boundary (full generics coverage is in its own guide).

function once any>(fn: T): T {
    let called = false;
    let result: ReturnType;

    return ((...args: Parameters) => {
        if (!called) {
            result = fn(...args);
            called = true;
        }
        return result;
    }) as T;
}

const initialize = once((config: string) => {
    console.log("Initializing with", config);
    return true;
});

initialize("prod");   // runs
initialize("dev");    // no-op, returns cached result
💡 Tip: Parameters<T> and ReturnType<T> are built-in utility types that extract a function's parameter tuple and return type respectively — invaluable when wrapping arbitrary functions generically.

ADVANCED10. Best Practices

1. Always Annotate Parameters

// ✅ Good
function process(value: string): void { /* ... */ }

2. Let Return Types Be Inferred for Simple Functions

// ✅ Fine to omit — obviously a number
function double(n: number) {
    return n * 2;
}

3. Prefer Union Parameters Over Overloads When Possible

// ✅ Simpler than overloads when return type doesn't change
function format(value: string | number): string {
    return String(value);
}

4. Name Function Types for Reuse

// ✅ Good
type Validator = (value: T) => boolean;
const isPositive: Validator = (n) => n > 0;

5. Avoid Overly Generic any Callbacks

// ❌ Avoid
function on(event: string, handler: (...args: any[]) => any) {}

// ✅ Better - specific to the event's real payload
function onUserCreated(handler: (user: { id: number; name: string }) => void) {}

📋 Quick Reference Summary

Concept Key Points
Parameter types Always required explicitly; never inferred from context alone
Optional / Default param?: T or param: T = value, must follow required params
Rest parameters ...args: T[], must be last
Function type expressions (a: T, b: U) => R — describes callable shapes
Overloads Multiple signatures for one function name, one implementation
this parameter Fake first parameter, erased at compile time, types this
Parameters<T> / ReturnType<T> Utility types for extracting a function's signature pieces
